body_markdown:
Carter Kramer will tell you he has friends who own cars for less time than their inspection stickers last. These people are always looking for something new. Kramer, however, relishes the feeling of owning a car that has been with him for half his life. “Sometimes, I have to remind myself that this is the same car I drove around in high school, zip-tied together.” The zip-ties are gone, but Kramer’s[1976 BMW 2002](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/bmw/2002/1976/1976-bmw-2002-base?id=aCn1I000000DTJgSAO) is still held together by half a lifetime of memories.


His passion for cars came early, but it wasn’t until he got to know a family friend named Mike Bruno that his trajectory was fully set. Kramer was 16 years old at the time, still impressionable, and Bruno drove a silver Alfa Romeo GTV.


“When I met Mike, I discovered my love of vintage cars,” Kramer says. “To me, that Alfa was the coolest car, and I wanted one so badly.” This was 2011, Kramer was about to get his license, and he’d decided he wanted a GTV for his first car.


Sean Smith


Bruno, however, infused him with a bit of realism. “Mike told me not to get an Alfa, that they were extremely unreliable.” Instead, Bruno steered him toward[a BMW 2002](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/your-definitive-1968-76-bmw-2002-buyers-guide/) , which his own son had just gotten. “That will be a great first car,” Bruno told him. After taking a ride in one, Kramer was sold.


As a New Yorker, however, he knew that all the 2002s close by had been eaten by rust. “Like a 16-year-old who knows everything and has the answer to everything, I found a 2002 in Florida and had it shipped up. Also, like a 16-year-old who knows how to drive like Ken Block, I was on a dirt road going around a turn, and I just thought I would kick the tail out a bit.” Instead, the BMW’s open differential sent him into a fence post. “I didn’t know it at the time, but that run-in took me on a fifteen-year journey with the car, and I wouldn’t trade it for anything.”


The insurance company valued the car at three grand. That was less than half what Kramer had paid only a few months before. “I thought, what am I going to do with $3000? I’ll just fix it myself.”


Kramer was handy. Before he’d learned to drive, he worked on bicycles, turning three bikes into one. He tinkered with lawn mowers and boat motors. “I thought to myself, ‘It’s a simple car, I’m sure I can figure out how to do this.’ So I jumped in the deep end. I had a pair of garden shears, a hacksaw, a crowbar, and a sledgehammer. I even went so far as to wrap a chain around a tree to pull out the front-end damage.” Kramer managed to cobble the car back together and then drove it, but the entire experience had taught him what to do—and what not to do.


Sean Smith


At 17, he started an internship at[Dominick European](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/lancias-are-the-treasures-at-the-heart-of-the-spadaro-family/) Car Repair in White Plains, New York. Armed with that burgeoning experience and the vast confidence inherent in 17-year-olds, he decided to take the car apart in his mom’s driveway so he could rebuild it again, only better. Except for one thing: “This time, I had taken it apart too far. I didn’t know how to get it back together.”


He and a friend put[the BMW](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/still-strong-at-60-the-bmw-02-series/) and its pieces on a trailer and brought everything to Dominick’s. He spent weekdays after school working on it, with the help of owners[Frank](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/picture-car-confidential/picture-car-confidential-35-eulogy-for-a-master-mechanic/) and Santo Spadaro. “Every day, they would help me put the car back together a little bit at a time. We got the car running again, so I spray-painted it Inka Orange just so I could drive it up and down the road.”


Just before Carter went off to the University of Rhode Island to study marketing and communications, he sold the 2002 and bought a 1998 5 Series for $1200, because he felt he needed something more modern. “I hated it!”


Then Kramer met Kirsten Tegtmeier, who would become his girlfriend and eventually his wife. She could see how much he loved that 2002, how he talked about it, so they pooled their money and bought it back, for $1500.


Sean Smith


Sean Smith


Sean Smith


“The new owner had not had much luck with it and told me to get it out of his driveway.” Kramer started working on it right away. He fitted new wheels and tires, added fender flares, then Plasti-dipped it in orange rubber paint. “On a hot day,” he says, “the paint expanded and the hood blew up like a balloon and popped.” He taught himself to vinyl-wrap it, in orange, of course, before finally settling on a $500 paint job he saw advertised in the Bronx.


“I thought, how bad could it be?” Turns out, it looked fine, and Kramer kept improving the car, fixing what needed fixing, making constant improvements.


In 2015,[he made a video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A85-YQsm6pY) with Petrolicious and shared his story of the car. The feedback, Kramer says, was enormous, and it led to the opportunity to go to the Quail, A Motorsports Gathering, in 2018. “It was mind-boggling to be going out to Car Week with my BMW. I got the money together to put it on a transport, and my friend Dimi from Overseas Autobody, whose dad had been the 2002 dealer back in the day, told me he would love to repaint the car before it went out to the West Coast. He went above and beyond to make the car look perfect.”


The following year, Carter, Kirsten, and BMW were invited to the inaugural Audrain Concours in Newport, Rhode Island, to compete in the “30 Under 30” category (where the owner had to be under 30 years old and spent less than $30,000 on the car). Carter was 25 at the time.


On the lawn at the Audrain Concours


Courtesy Carter Kramer


The little orange 2002 held its own among the prewar iron on the Newport Bridge during the concours tour.


Courtesy Carter Kramer


“I didn’t think I was going to win,” he says. “I had been working on the car for years on a budget and doing as much as I could myself. There was another guy who was being followed around by a film crew, because they thought he would win. I told my story, the judges liked it and the car, and they gave me the win.”


Kramer relished the experience, especially because Kirsten was there with him. She is just as much a part of the car as he is. “I used to work at a car-storage facility. I can’t count how many guys would show up in minivans to take their Ferraris for a drive because their wives didn’t know about them. It’s a lot more fun to include them than to sneak around. Better for the marriage, too.”


Courtesy Carter Kramer


After deploying the orange BMW as their wedding car in August 2023, Kramer knew it was time for an overhaul. “I had put a ton of miles on the car, so the engine I had built in high school was getting tired.” He met with the father-and-son team of Mario and Chris Langston at Vintage Sports & Restoration, in Bedford, New Hampshire, to have them build a stroker motor for him.


Kramer delivered the 2002 to them with a trunk full of parts accumulated over the years, including the limited-slip differential and five-speed transmission from a 320i. “It was like sending my dog off to a kennel. I was wondering what was happening and wishing for a webcam, but sometimes you just have to trust other people and know they will do the right thing for you.”


Sean Smith


Sean Smith


Sean Smith


Sean Smith


The 2002 was away for a year, and Kramer admits he was not used to not having it around. But then, he says, “it came home a completely different machine. It *looked* like my car, but better.”


Kramer and the ’76 BMW 2002 he bought as a teenager have grown up together. It no longer has a racing number on the side, for instance, and he’s abandoned the black-out trim. The seats, too, are more comfortable now, and the exhaust isn’t routed in front of the rear wheels, “so my ears don’t bleed when I climb out of the car.” But make no mistake, the car is still loud; it still pops. “We don’t go through turns like we used to. We don’t pretend to be Ken Block—we leave that to the pros.” But, like any great longtime companion car, he says it will never be finished.


“It’s like a house. You turn around, and there is something else to be done. Part of the fun of having a vintage car is thinking about what is next with it.”


Carter and Kirsten now share the 2002 with their daughter. “Someday it will be her Ultimate Driving Machine,” he says.


Sean Smith


The post[Half a Lifetime Tinkering with an Orange BMW](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/half-a-lifetime-tinkering-with-an-orange-bmw/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
